title: Given a singly linked list, reorder it so that the nodes interleave from the two ends: the first node, then the last, then the second, then the second-to-last, and so on. Do it in place. (LeetCode: Reorder List)

s1_definition.profdef: Reordering a linked list into the first-last-second-secondlast pattern combines three techniques: find the middle with fast-slow pointers, reverse the second half in place, then merge the two halves by alternating nodes. It runs in linear time with constant extra space because no new nodes are allocated, only existing next pointers are rewired.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reordering a linked list into the first-last-second-secondlast pattern combines three techniques: find the middle with fast-slow pointers, reverse the second half in place, then merge the two halves by alternating nodes. It runs in linear time with constant extra space because no new nodes are allocated, only existing next pointers are rewired.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a chain of linked statement pages and wants to reorder them so the reader sees page one, then the very last page, then page two, then the second-to-last, alternating from both ends inward. He finds the middle page, flips the back half around so it runs backward, and then zips the two halves together one page at a time, like shuffling two decks of cards into one.

**One line to remember:** Split at the middle, reverse the back half, then zip the two halves together alternately.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach stores all nodes in an array for random access, then rewires pointers by picking from the front and back alternately, which uses extra space proportional to the length. The elegant in-place approach uses three well-known steps.

First, we find the middle with fast-slow pointers: slow moves one node, fast moves two, so when fast reaches the end slow is at the midpoint. Second, we reverse the list from the midpoint onward with the standard previous-current-next reversal, so the second half now runs backward. Third, we merge the first half and the reversed second half by alternating: take one node from the first half, then one from the reversed second half, relinking next pointers so they interleave. We stop when the second half is exhausted.

A finance usage example: suppose pages are `P1 -> P2 -> P3 -> P4`. The middle splits it into `P1 -> P2` and `P3 -> P4`. Reversing the second half gives `P4 -> P3`. Merging alternately yields `P1 -> P4 -> P2 -> P3`, which is exactly first, last, second, second-to-last.

The senior-level nuance: splitting the list cleanly at the middle matters, because if we do not break the link between the first half's tail and the second half, the merge can create a cycle. A careful implementation sets the first half's tail next to null before or during the merge. The merge loop must handle odd lengths, where the first half is one node longer, by letting the leftover middle node terminate the chain. This reorder is a direct composition of the midpoint and reversal building blocks, which is why mastering those pays off here.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India renders a customer's statement pages as a linked chain, and a presentation mode interleaves pages from the front and back so a reviewer can compare opening and closing pages side by side as they scroll. Rebuilding the chain by copying all pages into an array wastes memory for long statements, so the reorder must happen in place.

Problem 2 — The reorder must not accidentally create a loop in the chain, because any downstream traversal would then hang, so the split between halves must be clean.

The code defines a `StatementReorderer` class with a `reorder` method that finds the middle, reverses the second half, and merges alternately. A runnable demo reorders a four-page chain and logs the new order.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the page chain `P1 -> P2 -> P3 -> P4`.

Step 1: The reorderer finds the middle. The slow pointer stops at P2, so the first half is `P1 -> P2` and the second half starts at P3.

Step 2: It reverses the second half `P3 -> P4` into `P4 -> P3`, and sets P2's next to null so the two halves are cleanly separated and cannot form a loop.

Step 3: The merge begins. The first pointer is at P1 and the second pointer at P4. It links P1 to P4, then P4 to P1's old next P2, advancing the first pointer to P2 and the second pointer to P3.

Step 4: The merge continues. It links P2 to P3, then P3 to P2's old next, which is null. The first pointer advances to null and the second pointer advances to null, ending the merge.

Step 5: The final chain reads `P1 -> P4 -> P2 -> P3`, exactly first, last, second, second-to-last, with no cycle.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 7:15:00 PM com.bank.statement.ReorderDemo main
INFO: Statement pages reordered (interleaved from both ends).
INFO: New order: [P1 -> P4 -> P2 -> P3]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: P1→P2→P3→P4
    │ middle → first [P1→P2], second [P3→P4]
    │ reverse second → P4→P3 ; cut P2.next=null
    ▼
  merge alternately:
    P1→P4→(P2) , P2→P3→(null)
    ▼
  result: P1→P4→P2→P3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reordering a linked list so the nodes interleave from the two ends, first node then last then second then second-to-last, is a clean composition of three fundamental linked list techniques, and I do it in place in linear time with constant extra space. The naive approach copies every node into an array for random access and then rewires by picking alternately from the front and back, but that uses linear extra space, so the in-place method is the stronger answer.

I proceed in three phases. First I find the middle of the list with fast-slow pointers, moving the slow pointer one node and the fast pointer two so the slow pointer lands at the midpoint. Second I reverse the second half in place with the standard previous-current-next reversal so it runs backward. Third I merge the first half and the reversed second half by alternating, taking one node from the front half and one from the reversed back half and relinking the next pointers so they interleave, stopping when the back half is exhausted.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a statement presentation mode. We rendered a customer's statement pages as a linked chain, and a reviewer wanted the pages interleaved from the front and back so they could compare opening and closing pages as they scrolled. The statements could be long, so copying all the pages into an array was wasteful, and the in-place reorder rewired the existing chain without allocating anything.

The senior-level point I stress is the cycle hazard. When I split the list at the middle I must break the link between the first half's tail and the second half by setting that tail's next to null, otherwise the merge can wire the chain back into itself and create a loop that hangs any downstream traversal. I also handle odd-length lists naturally, because the first half ends up one node longer and the leftover middle node simply terminates the merged chain. Being able to point out exactly where a subtle cycle bug would creep in, and how the clean cut prevents it, is what separates a robust production implementation from one that passes the happy path but corrupts the structure on an edge case.
